card.summary_ko: 『삼국사기』 열전에 실린 온달 이야기. 바보라 불리던 가난한 사내가 평강공주를 만나 장군이 되고, 신라와 싸우다 전사하기까지를 전합니다.
card.summary_en: The story of Ondal from the biographies of the Samguk sagi: a poor man called a fool marries Princess Pyeonggang, rises to be a general, and dies fighting Silla.
card.edition_ko: 中文維基文庫 「三國史記/卷45」 (온달 전 부분), 판 11121335, CC BY-SA 4.0 (원전은 퍼블릭 도메인)
card.edition_en: Chinese Wikisource, "三國史記/卷45" (the Ondal biography), revision 11121335, CC BY-SA 4.0 (original work in the public domain)

notes.ko:
**배경** 『삼국사기』는 김부식(1075–1151)이 1145년경 편찬한 고려의 관찬 사서로, 권45는 열전 제5에 해당하며 온달전은 그 끝에 놓여 있습니다. 평강왕은 고구려 평원왕(재위 559–590)의 다른 이름으로, 영양왕(재위 590–618) 때 온달이 아단성에서 전사했다고 전합니다. 이야기의 세부(우스꽝스러운 외모, 공주의 가출, 말 고르기)에는 설화의 성격이 짙어, 어디까지가 사실인지는 학계에서도 논의가 이어집니다.

**의의** 고구려의 3월 3일 사냥 제천 행사, 대형 같은 관등, 신라와의 한강 유역 쟁탈을 보여 주는 드문 자료입니다. 또 아버지의 명에 맞서 자기 뜻으로 배우자를 택하고 남편을 이끄는 공주상은 후대 문학과 설화에서 '바보 온달과 평강공주'로 널리 이어졌습니다.

**형식과 주제** 정통 한문 전기(傳)의 틀로, 인물의 신분과 용모에서 시작해 사건을 시간순으로 서술하고 마지막에 죽음으로 맺습니다. 주제는 약속의 무게(王者無戱言), 신분보다 마음이 맞음(苟為同心), 안목 있는 내조, 그리고 충성과 애도입니다. 공주의 말에는 고전 인용(一斗粟猶可舂…)이 섞여 있습니다.

**읽기 도움**
- 乞食(걸식): 음식을 빌어먹음.
- 士大夫(사대부): 관료 계층.
- 食言(식언): 말을 어김.
- 寶釧(보천): 보석 팔찌.
- 楡皮(유피): 느릅나무 껍질, 구황 식량.
- 大兄(대형): 고구려의 관등.
- 與…言懷(여…언회): …에게 속마음을 말하다.
- 窆(폄): 관을 묻다.
- 柩(구): 시신을 넣은 관.
- 본문의 -{『}- 같은 표시는 위키문헌 원문의 조판 흔적이며 뜻과는 관계없습니다.
notes.en:
**Background** The Samguk sagi ("Chronicles of the Three Kingdoms") is a state history compiled by Kim Bu-sik (1075-1151) around 1145 under Goryeo. Volume 45 belongs to the biographies (yeoljeon, no. 5), and the Ondal biography closes it. "King Pyeonggang" is another name for King Pyeongwon of Goguryeo (r. 559-590); Ondal is said to have died at Adan Fortress under King Yeongyang (r. 590-618). The story's details (his odd looks, the princess leaving the palace, the choice of the horse) read like folktale, and how much is historical is debated.

**Significance** It is a rare source for Goguryeo's third-month hunting rite to Heaven, its ranks such as daehyeong, and the struggle with Silla over the Han River region. The princess, who defies her father, chooses her own husband and guides him to success, became the well-known "Fool Ondal and Princess Pyeonggang" of later literature and folklore.

**Form and themes** It follows the standard hanmun biography (jeon): status and appearance first, then events in order, ending in death. Themes are the weight of a promise ("a ruler has no jesting words"), compatibility of heart over rank, shrewd support from a spouse, and loyalty and mourning. The princess's speech includes a proverb-like quotation about millet and cloth.

**Reading help**
- 乞食 (geolsik): to beg for food.
- 士大夫 (sadaebu): the official gentry class.
- 食言 (sigeon): to go back on one's word.
- 寶釧 (bocheon): jewelled bracelets.
- 楡皮 (yupi): elm bark, a famine food.
- 大兄 (daehyeong): a Goguryeo court rank.
- 與…言懷: to tell someone what is on one's mind.
- 窆 (pyeom): to lower a coffin into the grave.
- 柩 (gu): a coffin holding the body.
- Marks such as -{『}- in the text are leftover Wikisource typesetting codes and carry no meaning.

paragraphs.orig: 溫達，高句麗平岡王時人也。容貌龍鐘可笑，中心則睟然。蒙家甚貧，常乞食以養母，破衫弊履，往來於市井間，時人目之為愚溫達。平岡王少女兒好啼，王戱曰：「汝常啼聒我耳，長必不得為士大夫妻，當歸之愚溫達。」王每言之。及女年二八，欲下嫁於上部高氏，公主對曰：「大王常語，汝必為溫達之婦，今何故改前言乎？匹夫猶不欲食言，況至尊乎。故曰：'王者無戱言'今大王之命，謬矣，妾不敢祗承。」王怒曰：「汝不從我敎，則固不得為吾女也，安用同居？宜從汝所適矣。」於是，公主以寶釧數十枚繫肘後，出宮獨行。路遇一人，問溫達之家，乃行至其家，見盲老母，近前拜，問其子所在。老母對曰：「吾子貧且陋，非貴人之所可近。今聞子之臭，芬馥異常，接子之手，柔滑如綿，必天下之貴人也。因誰之侜，以至於此乎？惟我息，不忍饑，取楡皮於山林，久而未還。」公主出行，至山下，見溫達負楡皮而來。公主與之言懷，溫達悖然曰：「此非幼女子所宜行，必非人也，狐鬼也，勿迫我也！」遂行不顧。公主獨歸，宿柴門下，明朝，更入，與母子備言之。溫達依違未決，其母曰：「吾息至陋，不足為貴人匹，吾家至窶，固不宜貴人居。」公主對曰：「古人言：『一斗粟猶可舂，一尺布猶可縫』，則苟為同心，何必富貴然後，可共乎？」乃賣金釧，買得田宅、奴婢、牛馬、器物，資用完具。初，買馬，公主語溫達曰：「愼勿買市人馬，須擇國馬病瘦而見放者，而後換之。」溫達如其言。公主養飼甚勤，馬日肥且壯。高句麗常以春三月三日，會獵樂浪之丘，以所獲猪鹿，祭天及山川神。至其日，王出獵，群臣及五部兵士皆從。於是，溫達以所養之馬隨行，其馳騁，常在前，所獲亦多，他無若者。王召來，問姓名，驚且異之。時，後周武帝出師伐遼東，王領軍逆戰於肄山之野。溫達為先鋒，疾鬪斬數十餘級，諸軍乘勝奮擊大克。及論功，無不以溫達為第一。王嘉歎之曰：「是吾女壻也。」備禮迎之，賜爵為大兄。由此，寵榮尤渥，威權日盛。及嬰陽王卽位，溫達奏曰：「惟新羅，割我漢北之地，為郡縣，百姓痛恨，未嘗忘父母之國。願大王不以愚不肖，授之以兵，一往必還吾地。」王許焉。臨行誓曰：「鷄立峴、竹嶺已西，不歸於我，則不返也。」遂行，與羅軍戰於阿旦城之下，為流矢所中，踣而死。欲葬，柩不肯動，公主來撫棺曰：「死生決矣，於乎，歸矣。」遂擧而窆。大王聞之悲慟。

paragraphs.en: Ondal was a man of Goguryeo in the time of King Pyeonggang. His face was oddly lumpish and laughable, yet his heart was clear and bright. His family was very poor; he constantly begged for food to support his mother, and in a tattered shirt and worn-out shoes he went to and fro among the market streets, so the people of the day called him "Ondal the Fool." King Pyeonggang's youngest daughter was fond of crying, and the king would joke, "You are always crying and deafening my ears; when you grow up you will surely not be fit to be the wife of a gentleman of the official class, and I shall have to send you to Ondal the Fool." The king said this every time. When the girl reached the age of sixteen, the king wished to marry her to a member of the Go clan of the Upper Division. The princess replied, "Great King, you have always said that I would be Ondal's wife; why do you now alter your former words? Even a common man does not wish to go back on his word, how much less one of supreme rank. Therefore it is said, 'A ruler has no words spoken in jest.' Now the Great King's command is mistaken, and I dare not respectfully obey." The king was angry and said, "If you will not follow my teaching, then you cannot be my daughter. What use is there in living together? Go where you will." Thereupon the princess tied several dozen precious bracelets to her elbow and, leaving the palace, set out alone. On the road she met a man and asked the way to Ondal's house, then went on until she reached it. She saw his blind old mother, came forward and bowed, and asked where her son was. The old mother answered, "My son is poor and ugly, not one that a noble person may come near. Now I smell your scent, extraordinarily fragrant, and when I touch your hand it is soft and smooth as cotton; you must be a noble person of the world. By whose deceit have you come to this? My son, unable to bear hunger, went to the mountain forest to take elm bark, and has been gone a long time without returning." The princess went out, and at the foot of the mountain she saw Ondal coming with a load of elm bark on his back. The princess told him what was in her heart, but Ondal flew into a rage and said, "This is not a place for a young girl to walk; you are surely not a human being but a fox spirit. Do not press me!" He walked on without looking back. The princess returned alone and slept beneath the brushwood gate; the next morning she went in again and told the mother and son everything. Ondal wavered and could not decide, and his mother said, "My son is utterly lowly and not worthy to be a noble lady's mate; my house is utterly wretched and is certainly no fit place for a noble lady to live." The princess replied, "The ancients said, 'Even a peck of millet can be pounded, even a foot of cloth can be sewn.' If we are truly of one mind, why must we be rich and honoured before we can live together?" She then sold her gold bracelets and bought fields and houses, slaves, oxen and horses, and household goods, so that everything needed was fully provided. At the first, when buying a horse, the princess said to Ondal, "Be careful not to buy a horse from the townspeople; you must choose a horse of the state that is sick and thin and has been cast off, and then exchange for it." Ondal did as she said. The princess fed and tended it very diligently, and the horse grew fatter and stronger day by day. Goguryeo always held a gathering on the third day of the third month each spring, hunting on the Nakrang hill, and with the boars and deer taken they sacrificed to Heaven and to the spirits of mountains and rivers. When that day came, the king went out to hunt, and his ministers and the soldiers of the Five Divisions all followed. Then Ondal went along with the horse he had raised; in galloping he was always in front, and what he captured was also plentiful, none of the others equalling him. The king summoned him and asked his name, and was astonished and struck by it. At that time Emperor Wu of the Later Zhou sent out an army to attack Liaodong, and the king led his army to meet them in battle on the plain of Isan. Ondal acted as vanguard, fought fiercely and cut down several tens of heads, and the armies, riding the victory, struck with vigour and won a great triumph. When merit was assessed, there was no one who did not rank Ondal first. The king praised and admired him, saying, "This is my son-in-law." He received him with full ceremony and conferred on him the rank of Daehyeong (Great Elder Brother). From then on his favour and honour were all the more lavish, and his authority and power grew greater by the day. When King Yeongyang came to the throne, Ondal memorialised, "Silla has cut off our lands north of the Han River and made them its commanderies and counties; the people are bitter with grief and have never forgotten their parents' country. I beg the Great King, not despising me as foolish and unworthy, to give me troops; once I go I will surely bring back our land." The king granted it. On setting out he swore, "If I do not return to us the lands west of Gyerip Pass and Jungnyeong, I will not come back." He then departed and fought the Silla army below Adan Fortress, where he was struck by a stray arrow, fell forward and died. When they wished to bury him, the coffin would not move. The princess came, stroked the coffin and said, "Life and death are settled. Alas, let us go home." Then they lifted it and lowered it into the grave. When the Great King heard of it, he was grieved and wept.
